extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo two-part framework), focusing on whether claims provide an improvement to technology, use a particular machine or effect a particular transformation, and whether additional elements are well‑understood, routine, or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement consideration (claim/specification must show improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art. A conclusory assertion of improvement without necessary detail is insufficient. The claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement; the claim must include the components or steps of the invention that provide the improvement, though it need not recite the improvement in boilerplate language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult the specification and determine whether a technical explanation of the asserted improvement is present and whether the claim reflects that improvement (consider the claim as a whole under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)). Avoid oversimplifying claims or ignoring specific claim requirements. The judicial exception alone cannot provide the improvement; the improvement can be provided by additional element(s) or by additional elements in combination with the recited exception. Generally examiners are not expected to make a qualitative judgment on the merits of the asserted improvement — if the examiner concludes no improvement, the burden shifts to applicant to provide persuasive arguments and supporting evidence (e.g., a § 1.132 declaration) showing what the specification would convey to one of ordinary skill in the art (evidence cannot be used to supplement the specification). Examples (illustrative): McRO (specification explained how claimed rules automated specific animation tasks and demonstrated improvement); Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec (claims did not include limitations addressing asserted improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities (an improvement to computer functionality) or merely invokes computers as a tool to implement an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive indicators: specification discussion of prior art and how invention improved computer storage/retrieval or other computer capabilities; specific implementations or data structures recited in claims. Examples courts have indicated may show improvement include: modification of Internet hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpages (DDR Holdings); inventive distribution of functionality within a network to filter Internet content (BASCOM); methods of rendering halftone digital images (Research Corp. Techs. v. Microsoft); distributed network architectures to reduce congestion (Amdocs); memory systems with programmable operational characteristics (Visual Memory); technical details for transmitting images over cellular networks (TLI) (note: lack of requisite technical details can make claims ineligible); particular server structures for organized digital images (TLI); specific programming/design techniques to create menus (Apple v. Ameranth); security-profile generation improving virus scanning (Finjan); improved user interfaces with particular data selection (Core Wireless); specific interface/implementation for 3D spreadsheets (Data Engine); methods restricting software by license (Ancora). Negative indicators: claim scope that can be performed mentally or entirely without a computer; mere addition of a generic computer or general-purpose computer functions; mere automation of manual processes or mere speed improvements due to generic computer capabilities. Case examples: Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics (method wholly performable mentally); FairWarning (speed increase solely from general-purpose computer); Credit Acceptance (mere automation of manual processes); RecogniCorp (process could be practiced verbally or by telephone). In determining improvement, consider overlap with other considerations (particular machine, mere instructions to apply an exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to other technology or technical fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of improvements to technology applies across technologies (not limited to computers); an improvement to technology in life sciences or other fields may demonstrate patent eligibility when the claim reflects a new and improved technical way of achieving an outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., an improved economic concept) is not an improvement in technology. Courts have found eligibility where claims improved existing technological processes (e.g., McRO: improved computer animation via particular rules; Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect: improved method for preserving hepatocytes). Examples that may show improvement include: particular computerized method of operating a rubber molding press (Diehr); new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications); advances in content downloading for streaming (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV); improved digital data compression (DDR Holdings, Intellectual Ventures I); particular methods incorporating virus screening into the Internet (Symantec); components or techniques that generate new data (Electric Power Group); particular configurations of sensors and methods of using raw data (Thales Visionix); specific structured GUIs that improve transaction accuracy (Trading Techs. Int’l v. CQG); improved processes for preserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litig. Mgmt.). Examples that may not be sufficient include commonplace business methods on general-purpose computers (Alice, Versata), use of well-known lab techniques (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health Diagnostics), gathering/analyzing information by conventional techniques then displaying results (TLI), high-level delivery of broadcast content to devices (Affinity Labs), general email screening on a generic computer (Symantec), advances only to informational content (Affinity Labs), or selecting one type of content from existing types or using generic hardware functions (Affinity Labs). Claims must recite details about how a computer aids the method or the significance of computer involvement; merely adding generic computer components is insufficient. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for 'mere instructions to apply an exception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration (machine-or-transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more (Step 2B), consider whether the judicial exception is applied with or by use of a particular machine; the machine-or-transformation test is a useful investigative clue but is not a stand-alone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must still apply Alice/Mayo two-part test; a claim that passes Alice/Mayo is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test, and a claim failing Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it passes M-or-T. Relevant factors include: the particularity or generality of the machine elements (degree to which the machine can be specifically identified rather than 'any and all machines'); whether the machine implements the steps of the method (integral use vs. merely an object on which the method operates); whether the machine's involvement is extra-solution activity or only a field-of-use limitation (nominal contribution does not integrate the exception). Examples where machine particulars mattered: Mackay Radio (particular antenna structure), Eibel Process (Fourdrinier machine structure). A general-purpose computer performing conventional functions does not qualify as a 'particular machine' (Ultramercial v. Hulu, Eon v. AT&T); mere recitation of tangible components or adding a generic computer or 'specially programmed' generic computer does not automatically provide significantly more. Examiners should evaluate interplay with other considerations (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use/technological environment). See MPEP § 2106.03 for definition of 'machine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing — a transformation is a clue that the claim integrates the exception into a practical application or recites significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'article' includes a physical object or substance that must be particular; 'transformation' means the article has changed to a different state or thing (more than mere use or change in location). New/different function or use can be evidence of transformation. Purely mental processes or mere manipulation of basic mathematical constructs are not eligible transformations. Relevant factors when a transformation is recited: (1) particularity or generality of the transformation (more particular transformations likely provide significantly more); (2) degree to which the recited article is particular (generic recitation or 'any and all articles' is less likely to provide significantly more); (3) nature/extent of change in state or thing (change in function/use > mere change in location); (4) nature of the article transformed (physical/tangible transformations weigh more than intangible concepts); (5) whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation (a transformation that contributes only nominally to execution likely does not provide significantly more). Examples: Tilghman v. Proctor (transformation of fatty bodies into fat acids and glycerine); Diamond v. Diehr (transforming raw uncured rubber into molded products). Examiners should still apply Alice/Mayo test; M-or-T is a clue but not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Step 2B consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional element(s) beyond the judicial exception are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry; this consideration is evaluated in Step 2B of the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the additional elements are found to be well-understood, routine, or conventional, they do not supply 'significantly more' to transform an ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application. Examiners should analyze prior art/knowledge in the field to determine whether claimed additional elements are conventional and consider whether combinations of elements amount to significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.05(b)-(g) and related sections for interplay with other Step 2B considerations (particular machine, particular transformation, insignificant extra-solution activity, mere instructions to apply an exception).
